newsitem.title: PERU: Freed Peruvian hostages recount ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Freed Peruvian hostages recount ordeal.

text.p: Weary hostages freed by Marxist Peruvian guerrillas recounted on Saturday their grueling three-day ordeal and implored the government to relax its tough stance for the sake of some 340 captives still inside.

The 38 bleary-eyed and stiff men released by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels from the Japanese ambassador's residence on Friday evening were the first to emerge from the building for nearly 24 hours.

Still dressed in the suits they wore to the exclusive cocktail party stormed by guerrillas on Tuesday evening, they painted a picture of steadily deteriorating conditions in the stifling, overcrowded residence.
"My companions are suffering a terribly worrying pressure," said Manuel Romero Caro, director of the local Gestion newspaper.

The most pressing problem for the remaining hostages was the lack of basic services, such as water and electricity, which were apparently cut off in an effort to wear down the rebels' resolve, the freed men said.
"Cutting off the services does not affect the MRTA, they are used to it," said Alex Kouri, mayor of Lima's neighbouring port, Callao. "The only people who are affected are the hostages."
Pleas from inside the residence -- spelled out on hand-painted signs thrust out a window -- for services to be restored have so far not been answered.
Kouri warned that President Alberto Fujimori's tough line could be endangering lives. "There are elderly people in a precarious state of health," he said.
Despite the stressful conditions, the freed captives said spirits among the hostages were relatively high.
"We became quite house-proud. Every day we cleaned the house, including the bathrooms," said released Peruvian businessman Manuel Iga.

The hostages, all male since the release of about 80 women in the first hours of the crisis, have spent three nights sleeping on the floor and lining up to use the four bathrooms in the ambassador's home.

With telephone lines and cellular communications cut off, their only contact with the outside world has been watching the residence's five or six television sets. "We watched TV 24 hours a day," Iga said.

Spirits rose and fell as new developments were reported. Kouri recalled one tense moment when a local television station reported that preparations were being made for an assault on the building. "You can imagine how we all felt," he said.
The rebels, who spoke to each other by numbers to hide their identities, had not physically or verbally attacked their prisoners, said Fernando Matsuda, a student.
The numbers system indicated that there were at least 22 MRTA guerrillas including two were women, one of whom seemed to be about 16 years old, Kouri said.

Matsuda said that before the release of the last 38 hostages, 149 were being kept on the ground floor of the property and 231 on the first floor. The rebels had split the hostages up into different groups with diplomats and military officials kept in separate rooms in the upper floor, he added. Communication between the two floors was not allowed.

The MRTA rebels still held on Saturday morning at least 340 hostages -- among them top government and military officials, foreign ambassadors and businessmen -- and vowed not to surrender until their demands were met.
Fujimori, who has made no public statements on the crisis, spent much of Friday huddled with generals at a military barracks.
The freed hostages warned against any plans of a surprise attack on the building. "They (the rebels) are prepared to do anything," Kouri said.
